extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners (Office personnel) and patent applicants/attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed subject matter is obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, including the factual inquiries to be made, rationales that may support obviousness, search and claim-scope considerations, examiner documentation requirements, and how to treat applicant rebuttals and secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries (core framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective analysis for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 is based on the Graham v. John Deere factual inquiries: (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also evaluate objective evidence/secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, unexpected results) and weigh such evidence case-by-case. The Graham factors control the obviousness inquiry and may be reordered in particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must obtain a thorough understanding of the invention disclosed and claimed by reading the specification and claims to determine the scope of the claimed invention, and then determine what to search for and where to search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification' (Phillips v. AWH and MPEP §2111). The search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for
rubrics_metrics.description: Search should cover the claimed subject matter and also disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching/suggestion to combine, a preferred search is directed to finding references that provide such a teaching or suggestion if they exist. See MPEP §904.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search (prior art scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art for 35 U.S.C. 103 can be either in the applicant's field of endeavor or reasonably pertinent to the particular problem; art from other fields may be considered if reasonably pertinent or if design incentives/market forces would prompt variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow general search guidelines in MPEP §§904–904.03. Prior art is not limited to the specific problem the patentee was trying to solve; references that solve different problems or are from different fields may be relevant (KSR guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences between claimed invention and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret the claim language and consider both the invention and the prior art as a whole to identify differences between the claimed invention and the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2111 and §2141.02. All claim limitations must be considered when comparing to prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding as to the level of ordinary skill in the art should be included, explicitly or implicitly, and may be used as a partial basis for resolving obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include: (1) type of problems encountered; (2) prior art solutions; (3) rapidity of innovations; (4) sophistication of the technology; (5) educational level of active workers in the field (In re GPAC). The person of ordinary skill is presumed to know the relevant art and to possess ordinary creativity (not an automaton). Examiners may rely on their own technical expertise to describe such a person's knowledge and skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations / objective evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence relevant to obviousness (commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, unexpected results) must be evaluated by Office personnel and weighed on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be included in the specification, accompany the application, or be submitted timely during prosecution. Presentation of evidence does not automatically dispose of the issue; weight is determined case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel as factfinders; requirement to articulate findings and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are factfinders for Graham inquiries and must ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning the state of the art and the teachings of applied references; after findings are articulated, an explanation supporting an obviousness rejection must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 132 requires notifying applicant of reasons for rejection so applicant can respond. Clearly setting forth findings and rationale in an Office action leads to prompt resolution. Factual findings may include how a person of ordinary skill would understand prior art teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation: broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the specification (including claims) to understand what the applicant has invented (see MPEP §904 and Phillips v. AWH).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: combining prior art elements according to known methods (predictable results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported where prior art elements are combined according to known methods to yield predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a recognized rationale set forth in KSR and exemplified in MPEP §2143; use case law and prior art teaching to explain predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: simple substitution of one known element for another
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported by a simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitution that yields only predictable results can render claims obvious (KSR examples). Examiner should explain why substitution would have been made by a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: use of a known technique to improve similar devices/products/methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a known technique to improve similar devices, methods, or products in the same way can support an obviousness conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person of ordinary skill would have recognized the technique would improve similar devices predictably, the use is likely obvious unless application is beyond their skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (or product/method) that is 'ready for improvement' to yield predictable results can support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The readiness for improvement and predictability of results should be explained in the rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: 'obvious to try' with finite predictable options and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' may support obviousness where choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions would have a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR permits 'obvious to try' reasoning where the options are finite and predictable; examiners must articulate why a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: analogous variations prompted by design incentives or market forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field may prompt variations for use in the same or a different field based on design incentives or market forces; if a person of ordinary skill could implement a predictable variation, §103 likely bars patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art from other fields may be considered if reasonably pertinent or if it would prompt predictable variation (KSR). Examiner should explain the relevance across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) and related teachings
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references can support obviousness; TSM is a valid rationale but should not be applied rigidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR cautioned against overly rigid TSM; however, TSM remains one of several valid rationales. Examiners should look for reasons to combine references if they exist but may also rely on other rationales like common sense or market forces. Preferred searches should try to find references providing teaching/suggestion if present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections must provide articulated reasoning with rational underpinning (no conclusory statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Kahn and KSR: provide explicit analysis and avoid conclusory assertions. Examiners should explain why differences would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant reply obligations under 37 C.F.R. 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must timely, distinctly, and specifically point out supposed errors in Office actions and reply to every ground of objection and rejection; replies must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective traverse of a rejection based on factual findings must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred. Mere assertions that a prima facie case is not established or that common knowledge is unsupported are insufficient; examiner may repeat rejection and make next action final (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence submitted by applicants when reevaluating an obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations and other evidence; the Office must consider it and weigh it appropriately. The burden shifts to the applicant to show the Office erred or provide other evidence of nonobviousness once Graham findings are established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away: criticising/discouraging prior art effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art that criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed solution may 'teach away' and weigh against a finding of obviousness; mere disclosure of multiple alternatives does not constitute teaching away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case examples (e.g., W.L. Gore v. Garlock) showing that art teaching away can defeat a motivation to combine. By contrast, disclosure of multiple alternatives without criticism is not teaching away (In re Fulton). See MPEP §2123.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case requirements (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness, the examiner must show a reasoned basis (rationale) for why the claimed invention would have been obvious and account for all claim limitations; reasonable expectation of success may be required depending on rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2142–§2143 for examples: suggestion/motivation to modify, reasonable expectation of success, and consideration of all claim limitations. The mere existence of differences between prior art and invention does not establish nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying a particular level of skill not always necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only facts of record about the level of skill are found within the prior art of record, a specific finding of a particular level of skill is not necessary where the prior art itself reflects an appropriate level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Chore‑Time and Okajima: examiners may rely on prior art to reflect skill level. Nevertheless, ascertainment of skill level is important to maintain objectivity in the inquiry.
